member.name: P:TwinCAT.Ads.Server.AdsServer.SlowFrameDispatchThreshold
member.summary: Threshold above which the delay between receiving an AMS frame and starting to dispatch it to an indication handler is logged as a warning. Defaults to 50 ms; set to or a negative value to disable the check.

remarks.para: This span covers the time between the frame leaving the receive loop and the handler being entered. It is not observable from handler code, but it is where scheduling delays (ThreadPool starvation, GC pauses) show up. A handler that measures only its own duration cannot see it.
remarks.example:
Report every frame that waited longer than 10 ms:
server.SlowFrameDispatchThreshold = TimeSpan.FromMilliseconds(10);

member.remarks: A persistently rising value indicates that the handlers do not keep up with the incoming frame rate (backpressure), for example because handler code blocks.

member.name: P:TwinCAT.Ads.Server.AdsServer.UseAsyncReceive
member.summary: Selects the asynchronous receive loop instead of the default synchronous one.
member.value: true to await the socket, false (default) to block a dedicated thread.

remarks.para: The synchronous loop blocks one dedicated thread per connection. Because that thread is owned by the server and never taken from the ThreadPool, receiving cannot be delayed by ThreadPool starvation. This is the default.
The asynchronous loop parks no thread, but its continuations run on the ThreadPool and therefore compete with the frame dispatch work items.

Do not enable this on machines with few cores. The synchronous loop is remarkably insensitive to the core count: its worst case stayed between 6 and 10 ms at 1, 2 and 20 cores, with 0-2 lock contentions. The asynchronous loop has the better typical latency (worst case about 4 ms) but shows sporadic tail excursions once cores are scarce - about 70 ms in 1 of 8 runs at one core, and 898 ms and 997 ms in 2 of 6 runs at two cores, the latter accompanied by ThreadPool thread injection. It also causes far more lock contention (64-122 versus 0-2). Since the problem being solved is exactly such a tail excursion, the synchronous loop is the safer default.
Must be set before the server is connected.

member.name: P:TwinCAT.Ads.Server.AmsServerImplBase.UseAsyncReceive
member.summary: Selects the asynchronous receive loop instead of the default synchronous one.
member.value: true to await the socket, false (default) to block a dedicated thread.

remarks.para: The synchronous loop blocks one dedicated thread per connection for the lifetime of that connection. Because that thread is not taken from the ThreadPool, receiving cannot be delayed by ThreadPool starvation.

The asynchronous loop parks no thread, but its continuations run on the ThreadPool and compete with the frame dispatch work items. The synchronous loop is insensitive to the core count (worst case 6-10 ms at 1, 2 and 20 cores, 0-2 lock contentions), while the asynchronous loop has the better typical latency but shows sporadic tail excursions when cores are scarce: about 70 ms in 1 of 8 runs at one core, and 898 ms and 997 ms in 2 of 6 runs at two cores. Keep the synchronous default unless the target has enough cores.
Must be set before the server is connected.

member.name: P:TwinCAT.Ads.Server.AmsServerImplBase.SlowFrameDispatchThreshold
member.summary: Threshold above which the delay between receiving an AMS frame and starting to dispatch it is logged as a warning. Defaults to 50 ms; set to or a negative value to disable the check.

remarks.para: The time a frame spends between leaving the receive loop and entering the handler is not observable from user code, but it is where scheduling delays (ThreadPool starvation, GC pauses) become visible. Handler code that only measures its own duration cannot see this span at all.
The timestamp itself is always taken; it costs a single call per frame. Only the reporting is gated by this threshold.

member.summary: Asynchronous counterpart of , used when is enabled.
member.returns: The receive completion and the consumed bytes.

remarks.para: Almost all of the time the receive loop spends waiting is the idle period between two frames, waiting for the first byte of the next one. That is the wait which parks a thread for the lifetime of the connection.

This implementation awaits that idle period with a peeking () receive, which does not consume the byte, and only then hands over to the synchronous frame reader. Once the first byte of a frame has arrived the remaining bytes follow within microseconds, so the synchronous read no longer parks the thread across idle time. This keeps a single implementation of the frame parsing instead of duplicating it in an async variant.

member.summary: Maximum accepted size (in bytes) for the data payload () of a single AMS command.
member.remarks: SECURITY (ICS-383): is a 32-bit length taken directly from the AMS header and is fully attacker-controlled. Without an upper bound, a single small message can force the server to pre-allocate an arbitrarily large payload buffer (up to ~4 GiB), enabling a memory-exhaustion denial-of-service. 64 MiB comfortably exceeds any legitimate single AMS frame (large symbol uploads, sum commands and file transfers are chunked well below this), while capping the per-message allocation. Reason (Bug 322712): hosts such as the VS Code PowerShell extension pre-load their own, older copy of Microsoft.Extensions.Configuration. The binder then ran against a mismatched version of that assembly and failed with MissingMethodException: ConfigurationSection.TryGetValue. Reading the values through only needs Microsoft.Extensions.Configuration.Abstractions, which is far more version tolerant.

Limitation: only the scalar keys are read. The nested RemoteConnections, Mqtt, Json and EtherCAT sections are not evaluated by the server and stay unset. Do not hand the result to code that expects a fully bound configuration.

To revert once hosts no longer force a down-level Microsoft.Extensions.Configuration: re-add the Microsoft.Extensions.Configuration.Binder package reference for every target framework, replace the three RouterConfigurationReader.Read(...) calls with ConfigurationBinder.Get<AmsRouterConfiguration>(...) and delete this class.
